warehouses.title: Inventory 1 — Warehouses & the Stock Architecture
warehouses.desc: The Warehouse master and stock architecture in ZhiftERP: the Warehouse doctype field walk — tree position, Is Group, warehouse types, the account resolution, retirement by the Disabled flag at zero; the three-level tree design with a written naming convention and the three design tests; the transit, quarantine, and subcontract warehouses; the default warehouse resolution chain with the Item Defaults table and the monthly fallback read; the Bin — actual, reserved, ordered, and projected quantities, derived and never edited; and warehouse custody — the keeper list, the role separation, and site scoping.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Warehouses: scope and record structure
lessons.html:
This module covers the Warehouse master and the stock architecture in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: create Warehouse records with their full field set; design the warehouse tree with a naming convention; use the warehouse types and the special warehouses; wire the default warehouses across items and transactions; read the Bin record; and operate warehouse custody with named keepers.

What a warehouse is in the system. A Warehouse record is a named place stock can be. It is not necessarily a building: a shelf area, a cold room, a van, a quarantine cage, and stock held at a subcontractor are all warehouses if the business needs a separate answer to two questions about them — what is here, and who answers for it. One physical building commonly contains several Warehouse records.

What reads the Warehouse record.

1. Every stock transaction — Purchase Receipts, Delivery Notes, Stock Entries, and Stock Reconciliations all post against warehouses; a movement is always from and/or to a named warehouse.
2. The Stock Ledger Entry — every posting writes ledger rows per item per warehouse (module 5 covers the ledger in full); the warehouse is one of the ledger's two primary dimensions.
3. The Bin — the standing per-item-per-warehouse balance record (Chapter 6).
4. The stock reports — Stock Balance, Stock Ledger, Stock Projected Qty, and the module 7 analytics all filter and group by warehouse.
5. The accounting link — under perpetual inventory, stock value posts to the account the warehouse resolves to (Chapter 2's account field; module 5 covers the postings).

Custody. The stock function operates the records; each physical warehouse has a named keeper who answers for its contents (Chapter 7's custody list); movements between custodies are documents (module 2), and counts prove custody periodically (module 4). The standing programme rule applies from the first record: no stock change without its document.

Build order. Warehouses are created before items carry defaults and before any stock posts, because everything above links to them:

1. The tree designed on paper first (Chapter 3) — levels, names, types.
2. Group nodes created, then leaf warehouses under them (Chapter 2).
3. The special warehouses added — transit, quarantine, subcontract (Chapter 4).
4. The defaults wired (Chapter 5).
5. The custody list written (Chapter 7).

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Warehouse doctype field walk. Chapter 3: the tree design. Chapter 4: warehouse types and the special warehouses. Chapter 5: the default wiring. Chapter 6: the Bin. Chapter 7: custody and permissions. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Warehouse doctype
lessons.html:
Open Warehouse (awesome bar) > New. Complete the fields in order.

1. Warehouse Name. The name per the convention Chapter 3 sets — the location prefix plus the function: Central - Main Store, Ibadan - Stock Room, Central - Quarantine. The system appends the company abbreviation to form the record ID; the name entered here is the readable part, and it prints on every stock document and report.

2. Company. Warehouses are per company. On a multi-company site, each entity's stock lives in its own warehouse set; the legal separation rule applies to stock exactly as to everything else.

3. Parent Warehouse and Is Group. Warehouses form a tree:

• Is Group ticked makes the record a grouping node — it can contain child warehouses and cannot hold stock.
• Leaf warehouses (Is Group clear) hold stock and appear on transactions.
• Select the Parent Warehouse to place the record in the tree; the Stock Balance report rolls leaf balances up through the group nodes.

The rule: stock sits only at leaf level. A group node that was created as a leaf and later needs children must first be emptied — plan the tree before stocking it (Chapter 3).

4. Warehouse Type. The classification link (Chapter 4) — Stores, Work In Progress, Finished Goods, Transit, and the types the business defines. The type is a reporting and behaviour dimension; transit type in particular participates in the two-step transfer machinery (module 2, Chapter 4).

5. Account. Under perpetual inventory, stock value posts to an account. The resolution order: the account set on this field, else the company's default inventory account. Set per-warehouse accounts only where the chart's design wants warehouse-level value visibility (the accountant's decision, recorded); otherwise leave the field blank and let the company default carry it — a mixed pattern set without a decision produces balance-sheet lines nobody can explain.

6. Address and contact. Complete for physical locations that receive deliveries — the address prints on documents that route goods there.

7. Disabled. Warehouses are retired by the Disabled flag, never deleted: ledger history references every warehouse that ever held stock, and the reference must stay readable. A warehouse is disabled only at zero stock — the closing procedure is: transfer the balance out by document, verify the Bin at zero, then disable.

Verification per record. The name follows the convention; the company correct; the tree position correct with Is Group honest; the type selected; the account field per the recorded design; physical locations carrying addresses.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The warehouse tree design
lessons.html:
The tree is designed once, on paper, before records are created. This chapter is the design procedure and its rules.

1. The design inputs. List, per site the business operates: the physical rooms and areas that need separate accountability; the functions that need separation regardless of geography (quarantine, transit, subcontract); and who keeps each. The custody answer drives the structure: if two areas share one keeper and one answer, they are one warehouse; if one room has two accountable zones, it is two.

2. The level structure. Three levels cover almost every business this track serves:

1. The root — All Warehouses (the system's root group node, per company).
2. The site groups — one group node per location: Central, Ibadan, Akure. Group nodes exist for rollup reporting: the Stock Balance report at the Ibadan node answers the whole branch in one row set.
3. The leaf warehouses — the accountability units under each site: Central - Main Store, Central - Quarantine, Ibadan - Stock Room.

Do not exceed three levels without a written reason. Every additional level adds a click to every lookup and a decision to every transaction, and the deep tree that mirrors shelf geography answers no question the leaf plus the item's own location note cannot.

3. The naming convention. Written before the first record:

1. Site prefix first — every leaf name starts with its site: Ibadan - .... Warehouse pickers on transactions sort and filter by name; the prefix keeps each site's warehouses adjacent and a mis-pick visible.
2. Function second — Main Store, Stock Room, Quarantine, Transit, Cold Room.
3. No abbreviations that collide — the convention document lists the allowed site codes.

4. The per-company rule. On a multi-company site, each company gets its own tree from its own root. A shared physical building serving two entities holds two warehouse sets — the stock of each company in its own records, moved between companies only by the inter-company documents the Accounts track governs, never by an internal transfer that crosses a legal boundary.

5. The design review. Before creation, the paper tree is reviewed against three tests:

1. The custody test — every leaf has exactly one named keeper (Chapter 7's list is drafted from the tree).
2. The transaction test — every planned movement type has a from and a to that exist (the receiving flow, the branch replenishment, the quarantine path, the transit legs — module 2's movements walked against the tree).
3. The report test — the questions the owner asks weekly (stock per branch, value per site, quarantine holdings) each answer from one node or one filter.

The tree that passes all three is created in an hour and rarely touched again; the tree improvised warehouse-by-warehouse is reorganised annually with stock in flight.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Warehouse types and the special warehouses
lessons.html:
Warehouse Type records classify warehouses, and three special warehouses participate in specific machinery. This chapter covers both.

1. The Warehouse Type master. Open Warehouse Type (awesome bar) > New — short classification records: Stores, Work In Progress, Finished Goods, Transit, and any the business adds (Cold Chain, Quarantine). The type is selected on each Warehouse record (Chapter 2) and read by reports and by the transfer machinery below. Create the set once with the tree design.

2. The transit warehouse. One transit warehouse per company (or per route where the business wants route-level visibility), type Transit. Its role in the two-step transfer (module 2, Chapter 4): goods leaving a source site post into transit; the receiving site's entry posts them out of transit into the destination. The consequences:

1. Stock physically on a truck is visible in the system as transit stock — the Stock Balance report filtered to the transit warehouse is the in-motion report.
2. Transit stock belongs to nobody's shelf count — counts at both sites reconcile because the moving stock sits in neither.
3. A transit balance older than the longest route is a shortfall or an unreceived transfer surfacing — module 2, Chapter 4's standing read.

3. The quarantine warehouse. One per site that inspects or holds stock: type per the business's classification, name per the convention. Its role: goods that must not sell or issue — awaiting inspection, recalled, damaged pending decision — are moved there by document the moment the condition is known. The quarantine warehouse makes the hold visible and enforceable: the selling and fulfilment flows draw from the trading warehouses, and stock in quarantine is simply not there to pick. Module 3's recall procedure and module 2's damage lane both land stock here.

4. The subcontract warehouse. Where the business sends materials to outside processors (the Procurement track's subcontracting flow), the materials remain the business's stock while at the vendor — held in a subcontract warehouse per vendor or one shared, per volume. The warehouse makes vendor-held stock a visible balance with a custody answer, counted by statement reconciliation with the vendor rather than by shelf count.

5. What does not get a warehouse. Two non-cases, stated to prevent them:

1. Customers' premises — delivered goods left the business's stock at the Delivery Note; goods on approval or consignment follow the specific flows the Selling track defines, not an improvised customer warehouse per buyer.
2. People — a van or a technician's kit can be a warehouse (a place with custody); a person's informal holding cannot. Stock handed to a person without a document is module 2's first error, whatever it is called.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The default warehouse wiring
lessons.html:
Transactions pre-fill their warehouses from a resolution chain. This chapter walks the chain and the wiring procedure. A default is a convenience with consequences: every mis-wired default posts silently to the wrong place until a count finds it.

1. The resolution order on a transaction row. When a stock transaction line needs a warehouse, the system resolves, in order:

1. The warehouse typed on the row (always wins).
2. The document-level default (the warehouse set in the transaction's header, applied to new rows).
3. The Item Default for the item and company — the Default Warehouse row on the Item's defaults table.
4. The global default in Stock Settings (Default Warehouse).

2. The Item Defaults table. On the Item record, one defaults row per company: the Default Warehouse (plus the accounts and cost-center defaults the Accounts track governs). Wire it per the item's home: fast-moving retail items to the site store that stocks them; centrally-held items to the central store. On a multi-site business where every site stocks the item, the item default carries the central home and the site documents override at header level — the convention is decided once and written, because a register wired half one way and half the other pre-fills wrongly somewhere every day.

3. The transaction-side defaults.

1. Buying: the Purchase Receipt's Set Accepted Warehouse header default; the supplier-facing flows land goods at the receiving site's store, with the Rejected Warehouse set to the quarantine warehouse where inspection is in use (the rejected line posts there automatically — the wiring that makes Chapter 4's quarantine real at the dock).
2. Selling: the Delivery Note and Sales Invoice source warehouse defaults; the POS Profile's warehouse (the ZhiftPOS track, module 2) fixes each till's source — a till pointing at the wrong warehouse sells one site's stock from another's records, and the POS profile review carries the check.
3. Stock Settings: the global Default Warehouse is the last resort of the chain — set it to the main central store and treat any posting that fell through to it as a wiring gap to fix, found by the monthly read below.

4. The wiring procedure.

1. At implementation: the convention written (which level carries which default), the Item Defaults loaded by governed import, the transaction and profile defaults set, Stock Settings last.
2. At item creation: the defaults row is part of the item-creation checklist — an item created without its warehouse default pre-fills from the global fallback and posts to the wrong store on its first receipt.
3. The monthly read: the Stock Ledger filtered to the global-default warehouse for the month — every line that landed there through the fallback names an item whose wiring is missing; fix the Item Default, and move the stock by document if it physically sits elsewhere.

Verification. Sample five items per site: create a draft receipt and a draft delivery row for each and confirm the pre-filled warehouse is the intended one; delete the drafts. Ten minutes at go-live; repeated after any bulk item import.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The Bin
lessons.html:
The Bin is the standing balance record — one per item per warehouse, maintained by the system from postings. This chapter covers reading it, the projected quantity, and the Bin's integrity.

1. What a Bin holds. Open any item's record and view its stock levels, or open the Bin list filtered by item or warehouse. Per item-warehouse pair:

1. Actual Qty — the on-hand balance: the sum of every posted stock movement for the pair. This is the figure the shelf should match.
2. Reserved Qty — committed to submitted Sales Orders not yet delivered.
3. Ordered Qty — incoming on submitted Purchase Orders not yet received.
4. Indented / Planned Qty — requested on Material Requests / planned by production, where those flows are in use.
5. Projected Qty — the forward-looking figure: actual + ordered − reserved (plus the planning terms where used). Replenishment decisions (module 7) read projected, not actual — actual says what is on the shelf; projected says what will be after the commitments land.

2. How the Bin is maintained. Every submitted stock document writes Stock Ledger Entries (module 5), and the Bin is the per-pair running total of those entries. Two consequences:

1. The Bin is derived, never edited. There is no lawful direct edit to a Bin figure. A wrong actual quantity is corrected by the document that explains it — a Stock Reconciliation after a count (module 4), or the missing movement entered (module 2). An edit without a document would make the balance disagree with its own ledger.
2. The Bin and the ledger must agree. They do, structurally, unless damage has occurred (a failed patch, a crashed repost); module 5 covers the integrity checks, and a bin-versus-ledger disagreement is an incident for the sysadmin lane, not a figure to adjust.

3. Reading bins in practice.

1. The item view — one item across all warehouses: where its stock sits, what is reserved where. The first lookup for any where-is-it question.
2. The warehouse view — the Stock Balance report at a warehouse: the keeper's own holdings list, and the count sheet's source (module 4).
3. The negative check — a negative Actual Qty means more left than arrived in the records: either a movement was never entered or stock was taken without document. Stock Settings' Allow Negative Stock switch decides whether the system permits the posting at all; the recommended posture is off (the honest register refuses to pretend), with module 8 covering the setting's full consequences. Where negatives exist from history, the standing read lists them and each is closed by its explaining document.

4. Reserved-quantity hygiene. Reserved figures come from submitted Sales Orders; orders that will never fulfil (stale, cancelled by conversation but not in the system) hold reservations that distort projected quantities and block replenishment arithmetic. The monthly read: reservations against orders older than the fulfilment horizon, each closed or re-dated by its document — the Selling track's order hygiene, read from the stock side.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Custody and permissions
lessons.html:
Stock is money on shelves. This chapter sets who can do what to it, and who answers for each place it sits.

1. The custody list. One page, drafted from the tree (Chapter 3), maintained by the stock function:

• One row per leaf warehouse: the warehouse, the named keeper, the deputy, and the count cadence (module 4 sets the cadences).
• The keeper answers for the warehouse's contents: receives against documents, releases against documents, and signs the counts. The deputy covers absence — a warehouse whose keeper is on leave with no deputy is module 4's unmarked-location failure in stock form.
• The list is reviewed quarterly and at every staffing change; a leaver or mover on the custody list is a same-day update (the HR track's lifecycle events carry the line).

2. The role design. Per the Sysadmin track's permission rules, the stock roles at their standard shape:

1. Stock User — creates and submits the daily movement documents (entries, receipts, deliveries) within their site's scope.
2. Stock Manager — the elevated set: reconciliations, backdated postings where permitted, cancellations and amendments, the settings pages. The count-adjustment power in particular sits here, because a reconciliation moves value with one document (module 4's controls).
3. Read-only stock access — the reporting roles for finance and management.

The separation rule: the keeper of a warehouse does not approve their own adjustments. Counts are entered by the counting procedure's rules (module 4 — counted by one, entered against the sheet, the variance approved by the stock manager or owner per the threshold), so no single person can both hold the stock and rewrite its record.

3. Site scoping. Where the business wants branch users confined to branch warehouses, user permissions on the Warehouse doctype scope each user to their site's records — the branch storekeeper sees and posts to Ibadan warehouses only. Apply scoping per the sysadmin track's user-permission procedure and record it in the permission matrix; the quarterly access recertification covers the stock roles and scopes with everything else.

4. The document rule, restated as custody's mechanics. Custody changes only by document:

1. Into the business: Purchase Receipt (from suppliers), Stock Entry Material Receipt (the documented non-purchase cases).
2. Between custodies: Stock Entry Material Transfer (module 2) — the sending keeper's release and the receiving keeper's acceptance are the document's two sides.
3. Out of the business: Delivery Note (to customers), Stock Entry Material Issue with reason and approval (consumption, damage, write-off — module 2).
4. Nothing moves on a conversation. The stock handed over to be sorted out later is the origin of most variances module 4 will ever find; the document takes ninety seconds and the variance investigation takes a day.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: designing HealthTrade's network
lessons.html:
This chapter applies Chapters 2-7 to HealthTrade (the pharmaceutical distributor: Central/Lagos with the main operation, branches at Ibadan and Akure). Configuration values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the design inputs and the tree (Chapter 3). The custody walk of the physical sites lists: at Central — the main store, the cold room, the quarantine cage, the dispatch bay; at each branch — one stock room. The paper tree, three levels nowhere exceeded:

• All Warehouses (root)
• Central (group): Central - Main Store, Central - Cold Room, Central - Quarantine, Central - Dispatch
• Ibadan (group): Ibadan - Stock Room
• Akure (group): Akure - Stock Room
• Plus the specials at root level: Transit - HT (type Transit), Subcontract - Repack Vendor (the outside repacker holding HealthTrade stock).

The three design tests run: custody — every leaf one keeper (eight rows drafted); transactions — receiving, branch replenishment via transit, the quarantine path, and the subcontract leg each have their from and to; reports — stock per branch answers at the site group nodes, quarantine holdings at one leaf.

Step 2 — the records (Chapter 2). Warehouse Types confirmed (Stores, Transit, plus Cold Chain added); the group nodes created, then the leaves, names per the convention (site prefix, function). The account field left blank on all — the company default inventory account carries value, recorded as the accountant's decision. The dispatch bay is created as a leaf deliberately: loaded goods awaiting the truck have their own answer, separate from the main store's count.

Step 3 — the defaults wired (Chapter 5). Item Defaults loaded by governed import: retail pharmaceuticals default to Central - Main Store; cold-chain items to Central - Cold Room. The Purchase Receipt's Rejected Warehouse set to Central - Quarantine. The branch POS profiles' warehouses confirmed at their own stock rooms. Stock Settings' global default set to the main store; the monthly fallback read scheduled. The five-item pre-fill verification runs per site — one miss found (a cold-chain item defaulting to the main store; corrected before go-live rather than by July's count).

Step 4 — custody and roles (Chapter 7). The custody list finalised: eight leaves, eight keepers, deputies named for the three sites. The replenishment policy written into the procedures: branches replenish by transfer only — branch stock arrives from Central through the transit warehouse, never by direct branch purchasing outside the procurement lanes. Branch storekeepers scoped to their site's warehouses by user permission; Stock Manager held by two people at Central; the keeper-does-not-approve-own-adjustments separation recorded in the matrix.

Result. Ten warehouses, three levels, one written convention, eight custody rows, defaults verified by the pre-fill sample, and the special paths (quarantine, transit, subcontract) existing before the first document needs them. Module 2 runs a month of movements across exactly this network.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in warehouse architecture, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the person-shaped warehouse. Symptom: stock handed to people without documents; "with Emeka" as a location; variances at every count. Correction: the informal holdings documented into real warehouses or issued properly. Prevention: the custody rule — a place with a keeper can be a warehouse; an undocumented handover cannot, and nothing moves on a conversation.

Error 2 — the geography tree. Symptom: five-level trees mirroring shelves and aisles; every transaction a navigation exercise; reports that need six nodes to answer one branch. Correction: the tree flattened to the accountability units, stock transferred by document into the merged leaves, emptied leaves disabled. Prevention: the three-level rule and the three design tests before creation.

Error 3 — stock on group nodes and deleted warehouses. Symptom: attempts to post to group nodes; warehouses deleted with history and reports breaking. Correction: reposting to leaves; deleted records restored per the incident lane. Prevention: Is Group honest from creation, and retirement by the Disabled flag at zero balance only — never deletion.

Error 4 — the mis-wired defaults. Symptom: receipts landing in the wrong store; a till selling from another site's records; the global fallback collecting strays for months. Correction: the Item Defaults and profile warehouses fixed; misplaced stock moved by document. Prevention: the wiring convention written once, the item-creation checklist carrying the defaults row, the five-item pre-fill sample at go-live, and the monthly fallback read.

Error 5 — the edited balance. Symptom: someone "fixing" a quantity outside the document flow; the balance disagreeing with its own ledger. Correction: the change reversed and re-entered as the document that explains it (the reconciliation or the missing movement). Prevention: the rule that the Bin is derived, never edited — a wrong figure is corrected by a document, and bin-versus-ledger disagreement is a sysadmin incident.

Error 6 — the custody list nobody keeps. Symptom: warehouses without keepers; keepers who left months ago; counts nobody signs. Correction: the list rebuilt from the tree with current names. Prevention: the quarterly review and the lifecycle-event line — every transfer, promotion, or exit that touches a keeper updates the list the same day.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state what a warehouse is and what reads it; create a Warehouse record with the full field walk including the account resolution and the disable-at-zero rule; design a three-level tree through the three tests with a written naming convention; use the transit, quarantine, and subcontract warehouses and state what each enables; wire the default chain — row, header, Item Default, Stock Settings — with the monthly fallback read; read a Bin including projected quantity, and state why bins are never edited; and operate the custody list with the role separation and site scoping.

Module rule 1: a warehouse is a named accountability unit — designed into a shallow tree by written convention, stocked only at leaf level, wired into defaults once and verified, held by a named keeper, and changed only by document. Module 2 covers the Stock Entry and the internal movements.

stock_entries.title: Inventory 2 — Stock Entries & Internal Movements
stock_entries.desc: The Stock Entry and internal movements in ZhiftERP: the purpose walk — Material Transfer, Material Issue, Material Receipt, Repack, Send to Subcontractor; the full field walk including named Stock Entry Types, the rate rules per purpose, and the Difference Account; the issue and receipt lanes with their lawful cases, evidence, and approval ladder; one-step and two-step transfers through the transit warehouse with the shortfall procedure and the transit reads; Repack from the conversion register with the value-conservation rule; the subcontract despatch and vendor stock reconciliation; and the posting discipline — honest dates, backdating controls, the correction lane, and the monthly reads.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Stock Entry: scope and purposes
lessons.html:
This module covers the Stock Entry — the document for every internal stock movement in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: create a Stock Entry with its full field set; use each purpose correctly; run one-step and two-step transfers with the transit warehouse; operate the issue and receipt lanes with their reason and approval discipline; run repack conversions; move materials to subcontractors; and apply the posting rules that keep the movement record honest.

Where the Stock Entry sits. Stock crosses the business boundary on other documents — in by Purchase Receipt, out by Delivery Note (the Procurement and Selling tracks). Everything that moves inside the boundary, plus the documented exceptions at the boundary, is a Stock Entry. One doctype, several purposes; the purpose field decides what the entry does to quantity and value.

The purposes, in one table.

1. Material Transfer — stock moves between warehouses; total quantity unchanged, value travels with the stock (Chapter 4).
2. Material Issue — stock leaves the register without a sale: consumption, damage, write-off, samples; quantity down, value posts to the expense account the entry names (Chapter 3).
3. Material Receipt — stock enters without a purchase: the documented found-stock and non-purchase cases; quantity up, value posts against the account named (Chapter 3).
4. Repack — one form of stock becomes another: cartons consumed, retail units produced; total value conserved plus any added costs (Chapter 5).
5. Send to Subcontractor — materials move to the vendor-custody warehouse for outside processing (Chapter 6).
6. Material Transfer for Manufacture / Manufacture — the production flow's legs, used where the business runs work orders; the same mechanics with the production documents driving them.

Custody, restated for movements. Every entry has two sides or a reason: a transfer is released by one keeper and accepted by another; an issue or receipt is a boundary exception carrying its reason and its approval. The operator's rule from module 1 governs every chapter here: nothing moves without its document, and the document states what actually happened, on the date it happened.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Stock Entry field walk. Chapter 3: Material Issue and Material Receipt. Chapter 4: Material Transfer and the transit legs. Chapter 5: Repack. Chapter 6: Send to Subcontractor. Chapter 7: the posting discipline. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Stock Entry field walk
lessons.html:
Open Stock Entry (awesome bar) > New. Complete the fields in order.

1. Stock Entry Type / Purpose. Select the purpose first — it reshapes the form: which warehouses are required, whether accounts are asked for, how value behaves. The Stock Entry Type master maps named types onto the purposes; where the business has created named types (Damage Write-Off, Branch Replenishment) select the specific one, because the type prints on the document and filters the reports.

2. Posting Date and Posting Time. The date and time the movement actually happened. The honest-date rule: today's entry for yesterday's confirmed movement carries yesterday's date (Chapter 7 covers backdating's controls); an entry never carries a date chosen to land in a different period.

3. Source and Target Warehouse (header). The header values pre-fill every row:

• Transfers: both — from and to.
• Issues: source only. Receipts: target only.
• Rows can override the header where one entry genuinely moves lines between different pairs; prefer one entry per pair for readability.

4. The Items table. One row per item moved:

• Item Code and Qty in the stock unit (or the entered unit with its conversion — module 3's UoM rules apply).
• Basic Rate — on transfers and issues the system values the outgoing stock at the ledger's valuation rate (do not type over it; module 5 explains the rate); on receipts the rate must be entered, and it is a valuation event: the figure comes from the document that justifies it, not from memory.
• Serial / Batch — items under serial or batch control require the numbers on every movement (module 3); the row will not submit without them.
• Source/Target per row — visible when overriding the header.

5. The accounting fields. On issues and receipts, the Difference Account (per row or header per the configuration): the expense or income account the non-stock side posts to — damage to its damage/write-off account, consumption to its consumption account, per the chart the accountant governs. The account is part of the reason: an issue whose account says "Miscellaneous" has not stated what happened.

6. Cost Center / Project. Where the site addresses stock consumption to branches or projects, the dimension fields carry it — the Accounts track's addressing rules, applied to stock expense.

7. Attachments and remarks. The evidence per the lane's rule: the damage photo and supervisor's note on a write-off, the count slip on a documented receipt, the requisition on a consumption issue. Chapter 3 sets what each lane requires.

8. Save, review, submit. Entries are submittable documents: draft for review, submit to post. Submission writes the Stock Ledger Entries and the accounting postings; corrections after submission follow document rules — cancel/amend with the cause noted, never a compensating entry that hides the first one (Chapter 7).

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Material Issue and Material Receipt
lessons.html:
The boundary exceptions: stock leaving without a sale, entering without a purchase. Both lanes run on reason, account, evidence, and approval.

1. Material Issue — the lawful cases. Each case with its account and evidence, per the written stock policy:

1. Damage and expiry — goods unfit for sale: issued to the damage/write-off account, with the evidence the policy names (the photo, the expiry list, the supervisor's confirmation). Pharmaceutical expiries in particular follow the disposal regulations the compliance owner holds; the issue documents the stock side and references the disposal record.
2. Internal consumption — goods the business uses (cleaning materials, own-use items): issued to the consumption expense account against the requesting unit's cost center.
3. Samples and marketing — per the policy's line, to its account, with the recipient recorded.
4. Write-off after count investigation — module 4's lane: a confirmed loss the investigation could not recover, approved per the threshold ladder, to the shrinkage account.

The issue controls: every issue carries its reason (the named Stock Entry Type plus remarks), its correct account, its evidence attached, and its approval per the policy's threshold ladder (the keeper requests, the stock manager or owner approves by value band — the same decision/execution split as everywhere in the programme). The monthly issues read (Chapter 7) lists the month's issues by type, account, and value to the owner — write-offs are decided expenses, and the read is how they stay decided.

2. Material Receipt — the narrow lane. Receipts without purchases are rare by design; the lawful cases:

1. Found stock at count — goods physically present that the records never held, where investigation confirms no missing document explains them: received at the count's direction with the count sheet attached (module 4's lane — the reconciliation usually carries this; the receipt is the alternative where the policy prefers it for named cases).
2. Returns of issued goods — materials issued for consumption and returned unused, received back against the original issue's reference.
3. Opening exceptions — implementation-era cases under the go-live procedure, not a standing lane.

What Material Receipt is never used for: supplier deliveries (that is the Purchase Receipt, with the order, the supplier, and the three-way match the Procurement track runs — a Material Receipt for bought goods bypasses every purchasing control and mis-values the stock), and count adjustments where the Stock Reconciliation is the proper instrument.

3. The rate on receipts. A Material Receipt is a valuation event: the entered Basic Rate becomes ledger value. The rate comes from a document — the original issue for returns, the current valuation for found stock per the count procedure, the accountant's ruling for anything unusual. A receipt rated from memory plants a valuation error that module 5's reads will eventually excavate at many times the cost of checking now.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Material Transfer and the transit legs
lessons.html:
The transfer moves stock between custodies. This chapter covers the one-step form, the two-step form through transit, and the reads that keep transfers whole.

1. The one-step transfer. For moves within one site (main store to dispatch bay, store to cold room): one Stock Entry, purpose Material Transfer, source and target set, rows entered, submitted. The stock changes custody at submission; the sending and receiving keepers are the same site's team, and the document's two sides are the entry and the physical handover it records. Use one-step only where both keepers can verify the same physical event — which is what "same site" means operationally.

2. The two-step transfer through transit. For moves between sites, the movement takes time, and the record must be honest about the interval:

Leg 1 — despatch (Add to Transit). The sending site creates the transfer entry with Add to Transit set: source the sending warehouse, target the transit warehouse (module 1, Chapter 4). Submitted when the goods physically load: the sender's custody ends, the stock sits in transit, the despatch documents travel with the goods.

Leg 2 — receipt (End Transit). The receiving site creates the receiving entry against the despatch entry (the outgoing entry referenced, rows pulled from it): source the transit warehouse, target the receiving warehouse. The receiver counts the physical goods against the despatch rows and enters what actually arrived, then submits: the stock lands in the receiver's custody.

3. The shortfall procedure. When the receiver's count disagrees with the despatch (the carton that did not arrive):

1. The receiving entry records what arrived — never what the paper says should have. The difference remains in the transit warehouse as a visible balance.
2. The shortfall is reported the same day: despatch reference, item, quantity, to the stock manager.
3. The investigation runs (the loading record, the vehicle, the despatch count); the outcome closes the transit balance by its honest document — the late carton received when found, or the confirmed loss issued from transit to the shrinkage lane per Chapter 3's approval ladder, with the incident noted.
4. Nothing is "received complete and sorted out later": a receipt that pretends completeness moves the loss into the receiving warehouse's count, where it surfaces months later as the receiver's unexplained variance.

4. The transit reads.

1. Weekly: the Stock Balance report at the transit warehouse — every line is stock in motion; every line older than the longest route is a leg-2 entry someone has not made or a shortfall someone has not reported. Both are chased by despatch reference.
2. Monthly (with the close): transit ages to zero exceptions or each exception carries its open investigation — the month does not close over silent transit balances.

5. Transfer hygiene rules. One despatch entry per vehicle-load per destination (the receiving count matches one physical event); serial and batch numbers travel on the rows (module 3 — the receiver confirms identity, not just quantity); the despatch entry submits when the goods load, not when the paperwork is convenient.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Repack
lessons.html:
Repack converts stock from one form to another: cartons into retail strips, bulk into bottles, an assembled bundle from components. One entry, consumed rows and produced rows, value conserved.

1. The Repack entry. Open Stock Entry > purpose Repack:

1. The consumed rows — the items being broken down or combined: item, quantity, source warehouse. Valued by the ledger at their valuation rate, like any outgoing movement.
2. The produced rows — the items created: item, quantity, target warehouse, and the produced items marked as the entry's output per the form's flags.
3. The value rule — the produced stock's total value equals the consumed stock's total value plus any additional costs entered (below). The system distributes the value across the produced rows; where one repack produces multiple items, the distribution basis is set on the rows per the configuration, decided once with the accountant for each standing conversion.

2. Additional costs. The Additional Costs table carries genuine conversion costs where the business books them into the produced stock — the outside repacker's fee (Chapter 6's flow), materials consumed that are not stock rows. Each cost row names its account; the accountant rules which conversions carry costs and which absorb them as period expense. Do not use additional costs to "round" produced values to a preferred figure — the value rule is conservation, not target-setting.

3. The conversion register. Every standing conversion (PARA-500: 1 carton → 48 retail strips) is a written line: the consumed and produced items, the ratio, the batch handling (module 3 — the produced strips carry the source batch's identity per the batch procedure), and the distribution basis where multiple outputs. Repacks are entered from the register's ratios; a repack whose ratio disagrees with the register is a stopped entry and a question, because ratio drift is either a register update (the supplier changed the carton) or a leak (strips leaving between the carton and the shelf), and only the register makes the difference visible.

4. When Repack is not the instrument.

1. Damaged part of a carton — repack the good units per the ratio; issue the damaged units through Chapter 3's damage lane with its evidence. One event, two documents, each stating its truth.
2. Manufacture with a bill of materials — where the business runs real production (work orders, BOMs, operations), the manufacturing documents carry it; Repack is the light conversion without a work order, and the boundary between them is the business's process decision, recorded.
3. Unit-of-measure display — selling by strip from carton-stocked inventory may be a UoM conversion on the item (module 3), not a physical repack; use Repack when the physical form actually changes and the pieces need their own stock identity.

5. The repack read. Monthly: the month's repacks against the register — ratios matching, additional costs per the rulings, produced batches carrying their sources. Five minutes that keeps the conversion layer honest between counts.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Send to Subcontractor
lessons.html:
Materials processed by an outside vendor remain the business's stock. This chapter covers the movement, the custody, and the reconciliation.

1. The flow's shape. The Procurement track owns the commercial side: the subcontracting purchase order for the service, the vendor terms, the receipt of finished goods. This module owns the stock side: the materials leaving for the vendor, sitting in vendor custody, and being consumed into what comes back.

2. The despatch. Stock Entry, purpose Send to Subcontractor (created from or referencing the subcontracting order per the flow): source the business's store, target the subcontract warehouse (module 1, Chapter 4 — per vendor or shared, per the recorded design). Rows carry the materials with their batches; the entry submits when the goods physically leave, with the delivery documentation attached. The subcontract warehouse balance is, from this moment, the standing answer to "what of ours does the vendor hold".

3. The consumption. When finished goods return, the receiving flow (the Procurement track's subcontracted Purchase Receipt) consumes the sent materials from the subcontract warehouse per the order's bill of materials and lands the finished items in the business's store — the vendor's custody balance falls by what the production used. Where the site's flow uses explicit consumption entries, they post the same movement; either way the mechanics are the receipt's, and the stock operator's job is the verification below.

4. The vendor stock reconciliation. Monthly, per vendor with a subcontract balance:

1. The subcontract warehouse balance per item, from the Stock Balance report.
2. The vendor's statement of materials held, requested on the same date.
3. The two compared line by line; differences investigated to their documents — a despatch the vendor has not booked, a consumption the business has not received, wastage beyond the agreed allowance.
4. Wastage per the agreement is issued from the subcontract warehouse through Chapter 3's lane to its account (the agreed allowance is a term of the order, and consumption beyond it is a charge-back conversation the Procurement track owns — the stock records give that conversation its figures).

5. The subcontract reads. The monthly reconciliation above, plus the aging read: subcontract balances against the order's turnaround terms — materials at a vendor beyond the agreed cycle are the stock function's flag to the procurement owner. Vendor-held stock is the easiest stock in the business to stop watching, which is exactly why its warehouse, its reconciliation, and its aging read exist as standing structure rather than as memory.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The posting discipline
lessons.html:
The rules that keep the movement record trustworthy, gathered.

1. The honest date. Posting Date and Time state when the movement physically happened. Consequences:

1. Same-day entry is the standard: the despatch entered when the truck loads, the issue when the damage is confirmed. The gap between event and entry is where records and reality drift.
2. Backdating is the controlled exception: yesterday's confirmed movement entered today carries yesterday's date, by a user whose role permits backdated posting (the site's backdating controls per the sysadmin configuration), with the reason in remarks. Backdating into a closed period is refused by the close controls (the Accounts track's period rules); the movement that surfaces after close posts on the first open date with its remarks stating the physical date — the records honest about both facts.
3. Every backdated posting triggers revaluation downstream (module 5's repost mechanics — a movement inserted into history changes the valuation of everything after it), which is the technical reason backdating is a permissioned lane and not a habit.

2. The correction lane. A wrong submitted entry is corrected by cancel/amend with the cause noted, or by the explicit reversing entry that names what it reverses — never by a quiet compensating entry that leaves two wrong documents pretending to be right. The document trail must read as what happened: the error, its correction, the cause.

3. The draft-review rule. Entries above the value threshold the policy sets (and every reconciliation-adjacent entry) are reviewed in draft by a second person before submission — the same preparer/reviewer separation the programme applies to every value-moving document. The keeper prepares; the stock manager reviews the rows against the evidence; submission follows.

4. The standing reads, by cadence.

1. Weekly: the transit age read (Chapter 4).
2. Monthly, with the close: the issues read — the month's Material Issues by type, account, and value, to the owner (write-offs and consumption as decided figures); the receipts read — every Material Receipt with its lawful case named (the narrow lane audited by listing); the repack read (Chapter 5); the subcontract reconciliation and aging (Chapter 6); the backdated-postings list — every backdated entry with its reason, because a backdating pattern is a process gap at its source (the site that always enters Monday's movements on Wednesday needs its procedure fixed, not its permissions widened).
3. Quarterly: the Stock Entry Type census — entries by named type; a growing "other" or misused type means the type set no longer matches the business's real movements.

5. The evidence rule, closed. Each lane's required evidence (Chapter 3's table, the despatch documents, the count slips) attaches to the entry itself. The entry with its attachments is the movement's one-lookup answer — to the count investigation, the auditor's sample, and the question asked a year later — and the module's standing standard is that every movement answers from its document.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: a month of movements at HealthTrade
lessons.html:
This chapter runs one month of internal movements across the module 1 network. Configuration values and outcomes are listed per event.

Event 1 — the routine floor. The standing weekly movements run without incident: main store to dispatch bay one-step transfers as orders pick; cold-room replenishment one-step from the main store on the cold-chain list. Each entry same-day, header warehouses per the pair, no row overrides. The named Stock Entry Types (Branch Replenishment, Internal Move) print on the documents and feed the type census.

Event 2 — the quarantine path used in anger. A damaged shipment section is found at Central: a one-step transfer moves the affected cartons from Central - Main Store to Central - Quarantine the same morning — the goods are off the pickable balance within the hour. The inspection concludes two days later: part restored to the main store by transfer; the write-off portion issued from quarantine to the damage account with photos attached, approved by the stock manager under the threshold ladder.

Event 3 — the branch replenishment through transit. The week's Ibadan replenishment despatches: 40 cartons of PARA-500 plus twelve other lines, one despatch entry (Add to Transit) submitted as the truck loads, despatch documents with the vehicle. Ibadan receives next day against the despatch rows.

Event 4 — the shortfall procedure runs. On the same vehicle, one line — cough syrup — counts 18 of 20 loaded. The receiving entry records 18 (what arrived); 2 stay in transit as the visible difference; the shortfall report goes to the stock manager the same day with the despatch reference. The investigation: the loading record confirms 20 loaded; the vehicle check finds nothing; the confirmed loss of 2 is issued from the transit warehouse to the shrinkage account within the week, approved per the ladder, incident noted with the route and crew for the pattern file. The transit read the following Monday shows zero aged lines.

Event 5 — the repack cycle. The register's standing conversion runs twice: PARA-500, 1 carton → 48 retail strips, produced strips carrying the source batch. One entry's count proposes 46 strips from a carton; the entry is stopped per the register rule — inspection finds two crushed strips in the carton; the repack posts 46 good and the 2 damaged issue through the damage lane with the note. One event, two documents, each stating its truth.

Event 6 — the subcontract leg. The month's bulk lot despatches to the repack vendor: Send to Subcontractor into Subcontract - Repack Vendor, batches on the rows. Month-end: the vendor statement reconciles to the subcontract balance except one line — the vendor's booked wastage a fraction over the agreed allowance; the allowance portion issues to the wastage account, the excess goes to the procurement owner as a charge-back item with the figures attached.

The month's close. The reads run with the close: transit at zero exceptions; the issues read lists the quarantine write-off, the transit loss, the repack damage, and the subcontract wastage — four decided figures with four documents; the receipts read lists zero (the narrow lane stayed narrow); one backdated entry on the list (a Saturday movement entered Monday with Saturday's date and its reason). Every movement of the month answers from its document in one lookup.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in internal movements, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the undocumented handover. Symptom: stock physically moved on a conversation; counts at both ends wrong in opposite directions; the variance investigation reconstructing what a document would have stated. Correction: the movement entered with its honest date and remarks. Prevention: the module 1 custody rule operated — nothing moves without its document, and the same-day standard.

Error 2 — the receipt that pretends completeness. Symptom: transfers received "complete" regardless of the count; shortfalls migrating into receiving warehouses as later unexplained variances. Correction: the affected receipts traced, the losses moved to their honest documents. Prevention: the shortfall procedure — receive what arrived, leave the difference visible in transit, report the same day.

Error 3 — Material Receipt as a purchasing bypass. Symptom: bought goods entering by Material Receipt; no order, no supplier match, no three-way control; valuation typed from memory. Correction: the entries reversed and re-entered through the purchasing documents. Prevention: the narrow-lane rule and the monthly receipts read listing every receipt with its lawful case.

Error 4 — the reasonless issue. Symptom: issues to vague accounts without evidence or approval; write-offs accreting instead of being decided. Correction: the issues re-documented — reason, account, evidence, approval. Prevention: the lane table with its threshold ladder, and the monthly issues read to the owner.

Error 5 — ratio drift at repack. Symptom: conversions producing whatever the operator counts, with no register to disagree; leakage invisible between carton and shelf. Correction: the register written from the true ratios; recent repacks sampled against it. Prevention: the conversion register and the stopped-entry rule on any ratio disagreement.

Error 6 — the quiet compensating entry. Symptom: errors "fixed" by opposite entries that reference nothing; the trail reading as two unexplained movements; the auditor's sample finding both. Correction: the pair documented — what was wrong, what corrected it. Prevention: the correction lane — cancel/amend with cause, or the reversing entry that names its target.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the purposes and what each does to quantity and value; complete the Stock Entry field walk including the type, the honest date, the rate rule per purpose, and the difference account; run the issue and receipt lanes with their lawful cases, accounts, evidence, and approval ladder; run one-step and two-step transfers with the transit legs and the shortfall procedure; run repacks from the conversion register with the value rule; operate the subcontract despatch, reconciliation, and aging; and apply the posting discipline — backdating controls, the correction lane, the draft review, and the standing reads.

Module rule 2: every internal movement is a Stock Entry with its purpose — transfers received against what physically arrived, issues and receipts carrying reason, account, evidence, and approval, repacks held to their register, and every entry posted on its honest date. Module 3 covers serial and batch operations.
